items.title: The irony is that Attention is All You Need in 2017 meant that you could remove the recurrence from ...
items.content:
The irony is that Attention is All You Need in 2017 meant that you could remove the recurrence from the language model architecture that was considered SOTA at that time (e.g. LSTM with attention) and only keep the attention to get a model that would perform better because of the parallelism allowing training much bigger models.

Now we are in 2026 and we are putting the recurrence back into the transformer to make it smarter without making it bigger.

items.title: In long-context LLMs, there's a tradeoff: Transformer attention can use the full past but becomes ex...
items.content:
In long-context LLMs, there's a tradeoff: Transformer attention can use the full past but becomes expensive as sequences grow, while recurrent models keep a fixed-size memory whose update rule is itself a form of online learning.

This work, from researchers from @ByteDanceSeed_, @Princeton, @Tsinghua_Uni, @UCLA, and @hyperbolic_labs, argues that such memory should be trained using the representation that was actually available when a target was predicted, rather than the more common same-step pairing.

From that idea, the authors derive the Falcon family: normalized memory updates with explicit control over learning speed, forgetting, and whether each update uses one token or a short recent window, together with chunk-parallel implementations suitable for GPUs.

The experiments show competitive language modeling and better extrapolation on longer arithmetic sequences, making the paper useful as a precise framework for designing and reasoning about recurrent memory updates rather than treating them as opaque architectural choices.

items.content:
The best employee experience? Probably not humans competing with machines.

Better to design work so each does what it does best: let AI handle speed and repetition, while people keep judgment and responsibility in the decisions shaping the final outcomes.  

Microblog @antgrasso

Think of a claims team.

AI can sort incoming cases and summarize the documents. Good. Let it do that.

The specialist can spend more time on the cases where context changes the interpretation or an exception deserves attention.

But if the old workflow stays the same, something goes wrong. People may end up reviewing the AI output and still completing all the steps they were doing before.

Faster technology. More work for the employee.

Not exactly progress.

Work design has to decide where machine speed removes effort and where human judgment stays in charge. People should also know when they need to intervene and what they remain responsible for.

AI should take friction out of work, not give people another layer to manage.

A better employee experience is not less human work. It is less pointless work.

#EmployeeExperience #HumanCenteredAI

Training large transformer models often fails due to sudden divergence that wastes significant compute. Practitioners typically discover instability only after runs have already started, leaving them without reliable ways to assess risk in advance or adjust training proactively.

This work set out to develop a practical method for estimating the probability that a given transformer configuration will diverge before any training begins, and to turn that estimate into an intervention that prevents failure while allowing more aggressive optimization.

Does your AI know what matters to you?

Not what you told it. Not what's on your calendar. Not what you asked it to do last Tuesday.

What actually matters to you.

@ashwingop just published something worth sitting with. His argument: as models and execution get commoditized, memory becomes the moat. Not storing more — knowing what's worth storing. Knowing what's worth interrupting you for.

I think there's a harder question underneath that.

The calendar knows when. You know why. That gap...between what happened and why it matters... is where the next decade of AI gets won or lost.

On the day that Grok @bot can read my lists like https://t.co/...
items.content:
I was thinking about this all wrong 

On the day that Grok @bot can read my lists like https://t.co/8L5xphk0qQ does I will switch everything over to Grok Bot, which may be the product of the year.

Except the Tesla Roadster might beat it, albeit be unaffordable for most of us.

Wouldn’t it be a hoot if one in the Robotaxi network came to your house, picked you up, and took you to the race track. 

Then took you on the track and gave you a demo then took you home for $1,500. A lot more can afford than than $300,000-$600,000 for the ultimate robot, which is what I expect the Roadster to be priced at even though Ferrari sould out at $600,000 and the test will beat that in everything but design and that is still up in the air. I am expecting Roadster to gather crowds everywhere one goes.

That is what Audi charged for a day long class. Which are highly entertaining memories in my context store. :-)

Anyway, a guy who owns a Ferrari told me that often they hold their value even as they age.

Watch what happens to robot demand from here.

Waymo shows me. I am counting them along with others in EV industry. Growth going up exponentially.

Roadster could be more important than many are thinking.

And Cybercab will continue rolling out too slow for many entitled people in the Tesla community.

But it is more exponentially-growing its city count.

One today.

Another in two weeks.

Then another in four.

Then another.

But around that time they will switch to twice as many in the same timeframe.

That is your exponent.

We will see how fast that doubles.

But I was wrong to think there will be a price war.

Recently when interviewing @Waymo customers I have seen a sizable percentage lately of tourists who came to San Francisco to ride in an autonomous vehicle.

Like they keep telling me that is all they want to do.

They often come from places with lots of Luddite behavior. So they come to escape that and dream of a better future.

Which greatly excites me. 

Means that the nerds will soon turn from uncool to cool. 

And we need datacenters to bring them to yours.

But we have a fun way to change minds.

Give them three rides and then they will switch.

The thing is the Cybercab is not only cheaper to operate, but has a better experience. Many videos on YouTube bear that out.

So even if it charged the same price the network would be more profitable. 

Never bet against Elon.

But Waymo is in SF now, Tesla is not.

That worries me very little because Waymo will not be able to satisfy demand for years.

Everyone else in auto business should worry.

I was wrong about the price war, at least short term, maybe four years because economics shows that if demand goes up, but supply doesn’t, prices increase, but once it starts it will eviscerate everything else.

In 10 years you will be seen by most around you as an idiot if you are still driving in a manual gas car.

A Cybercab will be cheaper by then for all your average needs than owning your own car. And probably all the way to Yellowstone cheaper too. And way better experience. Like 100x better.

The future is fun. Even if I am wrong.

Except lately I have been amazed by what I see in labs and homes.

@GregMadison blew me away in his last week and now a few of us meet at parties to talk about what they experienced in his living room.

Robotaxi Racetrack.

I might be wrong, but the dreams are fun.
